newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's PM says Moslem group ready for projects.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's PM says Moslem group ready for projects.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan on Monday pledged a rapid start to commercial projects announced at a weekend summit of eight Moslem countries brought together under his initiative.
"These projects will be put into practice immediately," Erbakan told a news conference.
The summit brought together the leaders of Bangladesh, Egypt, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia, Nigeria, Pakistan and Turkey to launch the Developing-Eight (D-8) economic cooperation group.
The leaders agreed that Egypt would establish an international trade company, Indonesia would form a workshop on poverty alleviation and Iran would set up a D-8 technological data bank, Erbakan said.

He added that Malaysia would oversee the development of Takaful, or Islamic insurance schemes, Pakistan would be responsible for developing acquaculture projects and Turkey would produce aircraft for agricultural purposes.
Leaders of the eight countries said on Sunday increased economic cooperation among developing countries was essential if they were to strengthen their role in the global economy.
Erbakan acknowledged that existing economic links between members of the geographically diverse D-8 were limited.
"Trade between these countries is low. It does not amount to five percent of each country's trade," he said.
A D-8 declaration signed on Sunday called for moves to overcome trade barriers and establish joint business councils, while fulfilling existing international obligations of member countries.

Erbakan visited all D-8 countries except Bangladesh soon after coming to power last June. He fostered economic links with projects such as a $23 billion gas deal with Iran, drawing strong criticism from NATO-member Turkey's Western allies.

Political analysts say the D-8 group, devised as a potential developing world partner to the G-7 group of rich countries, has been ill-thought-out in Erbakan's haste to strengthen Turkey's links with the Islamic world.

Domestically, Erbakan's vision of Moslem brotherhood has been reduced to tatters by fierce opposition from the secularist establishment, which has brought his year-old coalition to breaking point and prompted him to seek early elections.
